These are playmates or social gatherings, or trinkets, or the amusements of people, and the kindness of people; these tear at him here and there, and pull at his heart and his inner self, so that he must necessarily rot in all divine life and in divine seriousness, and does not perceive God's grace and devotion. To a person, this little temptation is often much more harmful than the great afflictions, for the person guards himself against the latter with diligence and considers them to be wrong; but the person does not want to pay attention to these small faults, nor consider them to be wrong. In the same way that all things are much more harmful when they are not acknowledged than when they are, this danger, which one does not hold in much regard or pay attention to, such as social relationships, gatherings, or pleasure in creatures, is the same. Now, just as the deer is heated by every hunt, and its thirst increases all the more through it, so a person should be heated by every temptation toward divine love for our Lord, and should be spurred or driven by every affliction, in true thirst, to run more and more into God, where he finds nothing but truth, joy, justice, and comfort. <note>*) Ed. 1543.</note>

Now, the hunters sometimes do this: when the deer is too tired and too thirsty, they feed the dogs a little, and these are thus held back. When they are certain of the deer in the game park, they let the deer walk about a little, so that it is strengthened somewhat thereby, and then it can endure the hunting all the better. Our Lord does the same for the person. When He sees that the hunting is becoming too much for him, and the affliction too great, He holds them back a little, and then a drop is placed in the mouth of the person's heart. This is a sweet taste of the sweetness of divine things, which strengthens him so much that all things that are not God taste bitter and repulsive to him, and then he thinks he has completely and utterly overcome all his distress.

<summary>Tauler uses the allegory of a hunted deer to explain how minor, overlooked worldly distractions are often more spiritually dangerous than overt afflictions, and how God periodically provides spiritual relief to strengthen the soul.</summary>

To summarize everything stated thus far into one concept, it is necessary first to remind the reader: that the concern here is not the origin of experience, but rather what is contained within it. The former belongs to empirical psychology, and even there it could never be properly developed without the latter, which belongs to the critique of knowledge and specifically of the understanding.

Experience consists of intuitions, which belong to sensibility, and of judgments, which are solely a task of the understanding. However, those judgments that the understanding makes merely from sensory intuitions are by no means yet judgments of experience. In the former case, the judgment would only connect perceptions as they are given in sensory intuition; in the latter case, however, the judgments must state what experience is in general, and therefore not what mere perception, whose validity is merely subjective, contains. The judgment of experience must therefore, beyond the sensory intuition and the logical connection thereof (after they have been made universal through comparison) in a judgment, add something that determines the synthetic judgment as necessary and thereby as universally valid. It is immediately pleasant to anyone who possesses it (at least negatively, i.e., as the removal of all bodily pains). But in order to say that it is good, one must further direct it through reason toward purposes, namely that it is a state that makes us fit for all our tasks. In regard to happiness<note>original: "Glückseligkeit"</note> a), everyone finally believes that they can call the greatest sum (in terms of both quantity and duration) of the enjoyments of life a true, and indeed the highest, good. But reason struggles even against this. Pleasantness is enjoyment. But if it is designed for this alone, it would be foolish to be scrupulous regarding the means that provide it for us, whether it is obtained passively, through the liberality of nature, or through self-activity and our own efforts. But that a human's existence has a value in itself<note>original: "an sich"</note> b), if one merely lives (and is ever so busy in this regard) in order to enjoy, even if he were to be of the best service as a means for others who are likewise only out for enjoyment, and indeed because he shared in all pleasure through sympathy: reason will never let itself be persuaded of this. Only through what he does, without regard for enjoyment, in full freedom and independently of what nature might provide him even passively, does he give his existence as the existence of a person an absolute<note>original: "absoluten"</note> c) value; and happiness, with all the fullness of its pleasantness, is by far not an unconditioned good.*)

### *On the proportionality of the limbs.* Chap. CLXXV.

ALL the parts of any animal must be correspondent to its whole, meaning that a creature which is short and thick must have every limb in itself short and thick, and one that is long and thin should have long and thin limbs; and the one of average build must have limbs of the same average proportion. I intend the same to be understood regarding plants that have not been maimed by man or by winds, because these latter put forth new growth upon old, and thus their natural proportionality is destroyed.

### *On the junction of the hands with the arm.* Chap. CLXXVI.

THE junction of the arm with its hand diminishes when tightening, and thickens when the hand comes to open. The arm between the elbow and the hand acts in the opposite way in all its movements. This happens because, when the hand is opened, the inner muscles <term>muscoli domestici</term> <gloss>flexor muscles</gloss> extend and thin out the arm between the elbow and the hand, and when the hand is tightened, the inner and outer muscles <term>muscoli siluestri</term> <gloss>extensor muscles</gloss> retract and thicken. However, only the outer muscles move away from the bone because they are pulled by the bending of the hand.

<margin>Appearance of the city of Lima.</margin>
In this city there are good houses, and some are very beautiful with small towers and galleries. The market square is large, and the streets are wide, all leading directly to the market, from where one can see into every corner. On both sides runs flat land, and through the greater part of these houses run canals that bring in fresh water from the river, providing great convenience and comfort to the citizens, who can through this irrigate all their gardens and vegetable plots, which they keep clean and delightful. Also

<margin>Many water mills, with which they grind their corn.</margin>
there are many water mills on this river, in the manner of our own country, where they grind their corn. In short, very rich citizens live here, some of whom have 150,000 ducats. And from this city, ships sail at times with goods worth 800,000 ducats, and some even worth a million. On the east side, above the city, is a high hill upon which stands a crucifix. On another side outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep their beasts, their dovecotes, and their vineyards—though no good grapes, due to the nature of the land—and beautiful gardens, not only full of all kinds of fruits of that land, but also

Truly, to pass human life with joy—if the scandals, disagreements, and wars were not there—this place is certainly one of the most beautiful in the entire world, for the landscape there is so temperate that throughout the entire year there is no excessive heat or harmful cold. Also, one has never seen famine or plague there, or any rain, or thunderclaps, or lightning struck from the sky.

<margin>Why the City of Kings received its name, and was built in the year 1535.</margin>

Arriving at the coast, besides the fish, which they have in great abundance from the sea and the river, as well as meat and fruits of the trees and the earth, as has been said, there is no less abundance of wheat and grain. The four months that are summer in Spain are winter there, and a little colder than at other times. In these four winter months, there falls every day before noon a small dew or mist like a fog, though not unhealthy as it is with us: for those who have pain in the head, by washing themselves with this, find relief. Guaynacapa succeeded the aforementioned Lord; his name means wealthy or valiant youth, and he was both, more than any of his ancestors or successors. He was very prudent and established great order in the land everywhere. He was determined and brave, very fortunate in war, and achieved great victories. He extended his Kingdom much more than all his ancestors combined. Death overtook him in the Kingdom of Quito, which he had conquered, located four hundred leagues from his Court. Since these people and those who were coming with us were enemies and did not understand one another, we departed from the first group, giving them what we had been given, and went with the others. We stayed here one day, and the next we departed, taking them with us to other permanent houses where they ate the same as the others. From then on, there was a new custom: those who knew of our coming did not come out to receive us on the roads, as the others had done. Instead, we found them in their houses, and they had prepared others for us. Everyone was seated, and all had their faces turned toward the wall, their heads bowed, and their hair pulled forward over their eyes, with their belongings piled in the middle of the house. We also wanted to know where they had brought that maize from, and they told us from where the sun sets, and that it existed throughout that land, but that the nearest place was along that path. We asked them where we should go, and that they inform us of the road, because they did not want to go there. They told us the road was up that river toward the North, and that in seventeen days' journey we would not find anything else to eat except a fruit they call <term>chacan</term> <gloss>a type of edible root or fruit</gloss>, and that they crush it between stones; even after this effort, it is barely edible, so harsh and dry it is. This was the truth, for they showed it to us there and we could not eat it. They also told us that while we traveled up the river, we would always go among people who were their enemies and spoke their same language, and that they would have nothing to give us to eat; but that they would receive us with very good will and would give us many cotton blankets, hides, and other things they possessed. Nevertheless, it still seemed to them that we should by no means take that path. 

Doubtful as to what we should do, and which road would be most to our purpose and benefit, we remained with them for two days. They gave us beans and squashes to eat. The method of cooking them is so novel that, because it is as such, I wanted to write it here, so that it might be seen and known how diverse and strange are the inventions and industries of human beings. They do not possess pots, and to cook what they wish, they fill a large half-calabash with water, and into the fire they throw many stones that they can most easily heat. When they see them burning, they take them with wooden tongs and throw them into the water in the calabash, until they make it boil with the heat the stones carry. When they see the water boiling, they throw into it what they are to cook. During all this time, they do nothing but take out some stones and throw in others that are burning so that the water stays boiling to cook what they want, and this is how they cook it.
